overview.title: Banking Sector Reforms In India Basel Norms
overview.definition: Banking sector reforms in India encompass structural, operational, and regulatory changes initiated post-1991 to enhance financial stability, efficiency, and competitiveness, heavily anchored in international capital adequacy standards known as Basel Accords formulated by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS).
overview.importanceInUpsc: Crucial for UPSC CSE Prelims (RBI guidelines, Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio [CRAR], Basel III parameters, Prompt Corrective Action [PCA]) and Mains GS Paper III (Indian Economy, mobilization of resources, growth, development, and banking sector vulnerability/NPAs).
learningOutcomes: Master foundational concepts and mechanisms of Banking Sector Reforms In India Basel Norms.
Evaluate spatial distribution, institutional frameworks, and policy dimensions.
Apply high-yield mnemonics to solve tricky Prelims and Mains questions.
prerequisites: Basic understanding of commercial banking operations, assets, liabilities, and Non-Performing Assets (NPAs).

sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Narasimham Committee I (1991)**: Recommended reduction in SLR and CRR, phased entry of private sector banks, and introduction of prudential norms for income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning (IRAC norms).
• **Narasimham Committee II (1998)**: Focused on banking sector strengthening, further strengthening of capital adequacy norms, review of public sector bank autonomy, and merger of strong banks.
• **Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS)**: Headquartered at the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) in Basel, Switzerland; issues international standards for bank capital adequacy.
• **Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR)**: Also known as Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR), it is the metric that measures a bank's capital in relation to its risk-weighted credit exposures.

items.definition: Going-concern capital (equity capital and disclosed reserves) that absorbs losses immediately when a bank is operational.
Gone-concern capital (subordinated debt, hybrid instruments) that absorbs losses only when a bank is winding up.
A mandatory buffer of 2.5% (in addition to minimum CRAR) built during normal times to be drawn down during economic stress.
Ensures banks maintain an adequate profile of unencumbered high-quality liquid assets (HQLA) to meet liquidity needs for a 30-calendar-day stress scenario.
RBI framework that triggers mandatory and discretionary supervisory actions when scheduled commercial banks breach risk thresholds for capital, asset quality, or leverage.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **Financial Metros (Mumbai, Delhi, Bengaluru)**: Concentration of headquarters for Public Sector Banks (PSBs), All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs), and major foreign/private banks.
• **Tier-2/Tier-3 Expansion**: Driven by digital banking, payment banks, and small finance banks expanding credit access to unserved rural and semi-urban belts.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Capital constraints for PSBs, legacy NPAs, delays in full Basel III implementation due to economic headwinds, and liquidity mismatches.
• **Policy Interventions**: Recapitalization bonds, establishment of National Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (NARCL) or Bad Bank, amalgamation of PSBs, and digital transformation initiatives.

items.title: Mnemonic for Basel II Three Pillars
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: 'Min-Sup-Mark'
• **Decoded Meaning**: Pillar 1 = MINimum Capital Requirements; Pillar 2 = SUPervisory Review Process; Pillar 3 = MARket Discipline.
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Instantly distinguishes the core pillars when options mix up regulatory versus market domains.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: CRAR = (Eligible Capital [Tier 1 + Tier 2]) / (Risk-Weighted Assets [Credit + Market + Operational Risk]). Higher the risk, higher the capital required by RBI.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC often confuses Basel norms as legally binding international treaties passed by the UN. They are voluntary standards formulated by the BCBS, implemented in India through RBI statutory guidelines.

Mains Value Addition: In answers regarding banking resilience, emphasize that Basel III implementation in India has been conservative and robust, yet public sector banks frequently require sovereign capital infusions to maintain the mandated 11.5% CRAR (including CCB).

keyTakeaways: Banking sector reforms transformed India from a repressive, high-reserve regime to a risk-weighted, market-disciplined system.
Basel standards dictate capital adequacy across three generations (Basel I, II, III), with Basel III focusing heavily on liquidity ratios (LCR, NSFR) and systemic buffers.
Effective implementation requires balancing stringent prudential norms with credit growth needs of a developing economy.
